provenance.other: “the elements shall melt with fervent heat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Peter 3:10 and 3:12, and nowhere else in either Testament; the seven-word run is reproduced without a change. Two further elements of the same verse are present in the same sentence: 2 Peter 3:10 opens “the day of the Lord will come” against Moroni's “when the Lord shall come … that great day”, and closes with “the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up” — “the works that are therein” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — against Moroni's transfer of the burning to the earth. “day of visitation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 10:3 and 1 Peter 2:12, and Moroni's “the day of your visitation” inflects the Petrine one.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 3 is the New Testament's answer to people who say that nothing is going to happen — “Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (3:4). Mormon 9 is Moroni's answer to people who say that nothing happens any longer, that revelation and miracle are done away. He opens the argument by taking the scoffers' chapter whole: the fire that will find the elements, the day that comes as a thief, the burning of the works in the earth. Recover the context and the borrowing does the arguing — the epistle Moroni reaches for is the one written against exactly his opponents' premise, and its scoffers are refuted by a delay that is patience rather than absence. The chapter will return to the same page at 9:6.

9:2.note: 'That great day when the earth shall be rolled together as a scroll, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat.' Seven words verbatim from a two-verse KJV phrase, joined to a seven-word run from Isaiah 34:4 in the same clause and both of them handed to a question — 'then will ye say that there is no God?' The verse is a fusion, not a citation, and it is the densest single sentence of borrowed apocalyptic in the book of Mormon's own colophon. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold taken phrase by phrase, though the whole sentence is longer than it; category is quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's grounds — a complete predicate, absolutely rare, reproduced.
9:2.text: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

provenance.route: Isaiah 34:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon (second occurrence; see Mormon 5:23)
provenance.other: “rolled together as a scroll” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 34:4; “as a scroll” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 34:4 and Revelation 6:14. Revelation's syntax puts the participle after the noun (“as a scroll when it is rolled together”); Mormon 9:2 has Isaiah's order, as Mormon 5:23 does.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 6:14 is the same image in the same Bible and the better-known verse; the word order rules it out here for the same reason it was ruled out at 5:23.
provenance.significance: The book uses this phrase exactly twice, at Mormon 5:23 and here, and both times with Isaiah's word order and with Isaiah's noun changed from the heavens to the earth. That consistency is worth more than either occurrence alone: it shows the substitution is the text's own settled reading rather than a slip. What changes between the two is the addressee. At 5:23 the rolled-up earth is a threat held over the Lamanites — 'know ye not that ye are in the hands of God?' At 9:2 it is put to the deniers of God as a date: on the day the earth is rolled up you will be standing in front of the Lamb, and the question is whether you will still say there is no God.

9:2.note: Six words verbatim, one noun changed, in a verse that also reproduces seven words of 2 Peter 3:10. The two apocalypses are welded at the conjunction — Isaiah's scroll and Peter's elements share a single 'yea' — and neither source is named. Recorded separately from the 2 Peter row because the mediation differs: Isaiah reaches this verse in the Old Testament's own form while the rest of the sentence is New Testament, and a verse that draws on both Testaments in one breath is exactly the kind of thing the catalogue exists to make visible.
9:2.text: And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.

provenance.other: “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:12. Luke's parallel at 3:17 inverts it to 'fire unquenchable' and Mark 9:43 paraphrases it as 'the fire that never shall be quenched', so the compound adjective standing before its noun is Matthew's alone.
provenance.significance: John the Baptist's unquenchable fire burns chaff — the separated, worthless part of a harvest. Moroni's kindles on a man who has been made to see his own nakedness in the presence of the glory and holiness he denied. The transfer moves the fire from outside the person to inside him: what ignites is not a heap of chaff but the sight of oneself, and the fuel is the contrast between the nakedness and the holiness. It is the same move the chapter makes at 9:3-4, where hell is redescribed as a state of being unable to bear the company one is in.

9:5.note: 'It will kindle a flame of unquenchable fire upon you.' Two words, but the compound is a King James singleton in Matthew's word order, and it lands in a sequence (nakedness seen, glory seen, holiness seen, fire kindled) that has no equivalent in the Baptist's threshing floor. Filed moderate: the phrase is rare enough to name a source and short enough that a writer steeped in the KJV could produce it without reaching for one.
9:5.text: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

provenance.other: “blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 7:14 and 12:11. Only 7:14 attaches it to washing and to whiteness — 'washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb' — and Moroni has both, 'pure, fair, and white, having been cleansed by the blood of the Lamb'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 7:14 answers the question of Revelation 7:13, 'What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they?' — and the answer is that they came out of great tribulation. Moroni is writing at the end of a book whose people have just been destroyed, to readers he cannot see, and the verse he reaches for is the one that identifies the white-robed as survivors of a catastrophe. Note also what he does not take: Revelation washes robes, Moroni cleanses persons. The garment drops out, and with it the last screen between the man and the blood.

9:6.note: 'That perhaps ye may be found spotless, pure, fair, and white, having been cleansed by the blood of the Lamb, at that great and last day.' The paradox is the KJV's and Moroni keeps it whole: blood is the agent of whiteness. The chapter has been running on the Lamb since 9:2 ('brought to stand before the Lamb of God'), and this is where the Lamb stops being the judge one stands before and becomes the means of standing.
9:6.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “may be found of him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “found of him in peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both 2 Peter 3:14. The bare “without spot” occurs in exactly eleven, so the rarity here is in the construction — being FOUND in a certain condition on the day — not in the adjective.
provenance.significance: This row exists because of where it sits. Mormon 9:2 reproduces seven words of 2 Peter 3:10 and gestures at 3:12 and the burning of 3:10's close; four verses later the exhortation arrives in the shape of 2 Peter 3:14, which is the verse that draws the practical conclusion from exactly those verses — 'seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.' Moroni's 'that perhaps ye may be found spotless … at that great and last day' is the same sentence-shape with the same verb in the same voice, and it follows its source's own order: dissolution first, then the charge to be found unspotted. If 9:2 is a quotation of 2 Peter 3, 9:6 is the evidence that the whole chapter of it was open.

9:6.note: A weaker verbal case than 9:2's and it is not offered on its own. What makes it worth a row is sequence: the two verses of Mormon 9 that draw on 2 Peter 3 draw on it in its own order, four verses apart, and the second takes the very verse in which the epistle turns its apocalypse into a moral demand. Filed moderate because 'found spotless' is a phrase the Book of Mormon can produce unaided (compare Jacob 1:19, 'we would not be found spotless at the last day'), which is the reading a cautious editor should prefer.
9:6.whyNot: 'Spotless' is not the KJV's word here at all — 2 Peter has 'without spot' — and 'found … at the last day' is already Book of Mormon idiom by Jacob 1:19, three centuries of narrative time before Moroni. The row rests on the passive verb, the sequence and the neighbouring 9:2 rather than on any distinctive string.
9:6.text: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.

provenance.other: “interpretation of tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:10; “kinds of tongues” occurs in exactly one; “working of miracles” occurs in exactly one; all three are that verse. “gifts of healing” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 12:9 and 12:30. Moroni's list — prophecies, gifts, healing, speaking with tongues, the interpretation of tongues — runs the Pauline items in the Pauline order, 12:9 before 12:10, and closes on the phrase that exists nowhere else in the English Bible.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is in the verb Moroni gives his opponents. They 'say that they are done away' — and “shall be done away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:10, 'when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away', which stands eleven verses after the gift-list and is the sentence on which every argument that the gifts have ceased has ever been built. Two verses earlier, 1 Corinthians 13:8 says of the same list that 'whether there be tongues, they shall cease' — and “they shall cease” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, of which that is one. So the position Moroni is refuting is not a position he has invented for the purpose: it is 1 Corinthians 13:8-10 read as a timetable, and he answers it by putting Paul's own list back in Paul's own words and asking, at 9:15, 'Has the end come yet?' The whole of Mormon 9:7-20 is an argument conducted inside one chapter-pair of one epistle, and Moroni's answer to cessation is Paul's other verb: God 'has not ceased', 'he ceaseth not'.

9:7.note: 'They are done away, that there is no revelations, nor prophecies, nor gifts, nor healing, nor speaking with tongues, and the interpretation of tongues.' Three King James singletons from a single verse, taken in that verse's order, with a fourth from the neighbouring 12:9 — and the denial they are put in the mouth of is phrased with the verb of 1 Corinthians 13:10. This is the structural link of the chapter: everything from 9:7 to 9:20 argues the cessation question on 1 Corinthians 12-13's ground, and 9:15's 'Has the end come yet?' is a direct challenge to 13:10's 'when that which is perfect is come'. Moroni will make the same list again, and at greater length, at Moroni 10:8-18.
9:7.text: To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:

provenance.other: “ye know not the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 12:24; Matthew's parallel reads “not knowing the scriptures”, which also occurs in exactly one. Both are the same rebuke of the Sadducees and both pair scripture-ignorance with 'the power of God' — the phrase Moroni's chapter turns into its refrain from 9:17 onward.
provenance.significance: Read Mormon 9:8-11 straight through and it reproduces the shape of Mark 12:24-26 clause by clause. Mark: you err because you know not the scriptures, neither the power of God (12:24) … have ye not READ in the book of Moses (12:26) … I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Mormon: he 'knoweth not the Gospel of Christ; yea, they have not read the Scriptures' (9:8) … 'For do we not READ that God is the same yesterday' (9:9) … 'the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (9:11). Three steps in three verses in the same order, and the third of them carries the New Testament's own punctuation of the divine title rather than Exodus's (see the row at 9:11). Recover the source and the polemic acquires a target it does not name: in Mark the people who cannot read their own scriptures are the party that denies the resurrection, and in Mormon 9 they are the party that denies revelation and miracle. The argument Moroni makes at 9:13 — that Christ's death brings the resurrection to pass — is the argument Mark 12 is about.

9:8.note: 'He that denieth these things, knoweth not the Gospel of Christ; yea, they have not read the Scriptures; if so, they do not understand them.' No clause is reproduced, which is why this is an allusion rather than a quotation, and the case rests on sequence rather than volume: the rebuke, the not-having-read, and the God of Abraham arrive in Mark's order across four verses, and the middle term is unnecessary to Moroni's argument unless the pattern is being followed. Note the 1830 grammar the 1920 edition tidied away — 'he that denieth … they have not read … they do not understand' — which is worth keeping in view because the plural is what makes the sentence a rebuke of a party rather than of a man.
9:8.text: And Jesus answering said unto them, Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?

provenance.other: “the same yesterday” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:8, 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.' The 1830 prints 'to-day', hyphenated, against the modern edition's 'today' — the King James spacing survives in the first edition and was normalised later (CONVENTIONS §8). Malachi 3:6, 'I am the LORD, I change not', is the Old Testament's statement of the same doctrine and shares not one word of the formula; Moroni will paraphrase it separately at 9:19, 'He changeth not'.
provenance.significance: This is the only place in Mormon 9 where the borrowing is announced as a borrowing. 'For do we not READ that God is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever' is a citation formula, and it is the second step of the Mark 12:24-26 sequence identified at 9:8: the man who has not read the scriptures is now told what the scriptures say. What he is told is a fusion of two epistles neither of which is named, and the fusion is doing doctrinal work — Hebrews 13:8 predicates immutability of Jesus Christ, James 1:17 of the Father of lights, and Moroni's subject is simply 'God', so the seam between the two verses is exactly where the chapter's Father-and-Son identification at 9:12 will sit.

9:9.note: Six words reproduced without variation from a KJV singleton, and spliced in the same sentence to a second singleton from James 1:17. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold as a single run and so not one of his King James quotations, but the composite sentence is longer than it and reproduces two whole predicates from two different epistles. Hardy's apparatus cross-references both verses here, which is one of the few rows in this chapter that is not ours alone.
9:9.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

provenance.other: “no variableness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “shadow of turning” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both James 1:17. Moroni reproduces the first exactly and alters the second by a single noun: 'neither shadow of changing' for 'neither shadow of turning'.
provenance.significance: The substituted noun is not neutral. 'Turning' in James is an astronomical figure — the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation caused by the turning of the heavens — and 'changing' drops the figure to state the doctrine flat. Moroni then builds the next verse on the word he substituted: 'if ye have imagined up unto yourselves a god which doth vary, and in him there is shadow of changing, then have ye imagined up unto yourselves a god which is not a God of miracles' (9:10). The whole argument of 9:9-19 turns on the identity of immutability with continuing miracle: a God who has stopped working miracles has changed, and a God who changes is not God. That inference is Moroni's, not James's, and it is made possible by the one word he moved.

9:9.note: 'And in him there is no variableness, neither shadow of changing.' Nine words, of which eight are verbatim from a verse containing two King James singletons, and the ninth is a deliberate substitution that the next verse then quotes back. Hardy cross-references James 1:17 at this verse alongside Hebrews 13:8; the two are catalogued separately here because they are two sources fused in one sentence and the argument treats them differently — Hebrews supplies the citation formula's content, James supplies the vocabulary the chapter goes on to use.
9:9.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6 → the Synoptic resurrection controversy (Matthew 22:32 / Mark 12:26 / Luke 20:37) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Exodus 3:6 — 'I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.'
provenance.other: The punctuation of the triple decides this and the counts are absolute. “God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” — with the conjunction after Abraham — occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37 and Acts 7:32, every one of them New Testament. “God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” — without it — occurs in exactly three, Exodus 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5, every one of them Old Testament. Mormon 9:11 has the first. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Matthew 22:32 over Exodus 3:6 and none the other way.
provenance.significance: A one-word difference settles a route, which is why the count is given in full. But the finding is larger than the conjunction. Of the four New Testament verses that carry this form, three are the same pericope — Jesus answering the Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, by pointing out that God calls himself the God of the patriarchs and 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living'. Moroni has been inside that pericope since 9:8 ('they have not read the Scriptures' = Mark 12:24; 'do we not read' = Mark 12:26's 'have ye not read'), and he arrives at its punchline in its New Testament wording. What he does with it is his own: where the Synoptics use the title to prove the resurrection, Moroni uses it to prove that God still works miracles, and then extends it — 'and it is that same God which created the heavens and the earth' — so that the God who spoke at the bush is identified with the creator and the argument from the fathers becomes an argument from creation.

9:11.note: 'Even the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Fourteen words shared with four New Testament verses and with no Old Testament verse, on the strength of one conjunction. This is the chapter's cleanest mediation finding: the formula is Exodus's, the wording is the Gospels', and the surrounding argument has been tracking Mark 12:24-26 for three verses. Not a quotation — the clause is a title, not a predicate — but the reproduction is exact and the discrimination is decisive.
9:11.text: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:11 or Acts 4:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the two cannot be separated on this verse's evidence
provenance.other: “all that in them is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:11 (the sabbath commandment's creation clause) and Acts 4:24 (the apostles' prayer after the release of Peter and John). The two read identically at every point Mormon 9:11 reproduces, so tools/mediation-check.py can return nothing decisive; both differ from Moroni in supplying 'the sea', which he omits, and Acts 14:15's variant 'all things that are therein' is a third, further-off possibility.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence here, and it is a clean instance of CONVENTIONS §8. The first edition prints 'all things that in them IS' — the King James's own singular verb after a plural subject, which is what makes 'all that in them is' recognisable as a quotation rather than a paraphrase — and the 1920 edition corrected it to 'are'. The correction is grammatically right and it erases the borrowing: the modern text no longer contains the KJV's clause. So the 1830 shows a dependence the current edition has silently removed, and it shows it in the direction opposite to the usual editorial drift, since here the later edition moves AWAY from the source rather than toward it. Compare 1 Nephi 1:20, where the 1920 moved the other way.

9:11.note: 'And it is that same God which created the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is.' Five words, but they are five words in an ungrammatical arrangement that no writer produces by accident and that occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Mediation is recorded as uncertain and this is a real undecidedness rather than a shrug: Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24 are word-for-word identical across the whole of what Moroni reproduces, so the verse cannot settle its own route. Context pulls both ways — the chapter's stratum is heavily New Testament, which favours Acts, but the immediately preceding clause is the God of the burning bush, which favours the Decalogue's creation formula. Filed moderate on that account, not on the verbal evidence, which is strong.
9:11.text: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

provenance.route: Revelation 20:12, with 1 Corinthians 15:52 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “stand before God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12, 'And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God' — the bare 'small and great' is common, occurring in exactly thirteen verses, so it is the collocation with standing and with the dead that identifies the source. “the trumpet shall sound” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:52, where it is likewise followed immediately by the raising of the dead. The Book of Mormon reads 'the trump shall sound', which is 1 Thessalonians 4:16's noun in 1 Corinthians 15:52's clause.
provenance.significance: Moroni changes one word and the change is the doctrine: Revelation's dead stand before God, Moroni's stand before his BAR. The judicial furniture is the Book of Mormon's own — the phrase recurs across the book — and importing it here converts John's vision of opened books into a courtroom. What survives untouched is the pairing that made Revelation 20:12 worth taking: everyone rises, and the small rise with the great. Moroni is arguing against people who deny that God still acts, and the resurrection he offers as proof is one in which no one is exempted by insignificance.

9:13.note: 'All men shall be awoke by the power of God, when the trump shall sound; and they shall come forth, both small and great, and all shall stand before his bar.' Two New Testament resurrection texts fused in one clause, each identified by a King James singleton, and the seam is visible: the trumpet is Paul's, the small-and-great standing is John's. The 1830's 'awoke' for the modern 'awakened' is worth noting as a first-edition reading, though nothing in the judgment turns on it.
9:13.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “filthy still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “righteous still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Revelation 22:11. The Book of Mormon uses the pair twice and only twice, at 2 Nephi 9:16 and here.
provenance.significance: Moroni keeps two of John's four terms and replaces the other two. Revelation runs unjust / filthy / righteous / holy — a legal term, a cultic term, and two more of each — and its logic is that the door has closed and no one changes category any more. Moroni runs filthy / righteous / happy / unhappy, and the substitution of the last pair is the whole point of his version: it converts a statement about verdicts into a statement about states, and it is the same move he made at 9:3-4, where the misery of the damned is being unable to bear the company of a holy God rather than a sentence pronounced on them. Note too where the pair drops out of the Book of Mormon: Jacob quotes John's own terms at 2 Nephi 9:16 and follows them with the lake of fire, which is Revelation's furniture; Moroni quotes them and follows them with unhappiness, which is not.

9:14.note: 'He that is filthy, shall be filthy still; and he that is righteous, shall be righteous still: he that is happy, shall be happy still; and he that is unhappy, shall be unhappy still.' Two complete predicates reproduced from a verse containing two King James singletons, with the KJV's jussive ('let him be') flattened to a plain future — and then extended by two clauses of Moroni's own built on the borrowed frame. Category is quotation on the reproduced predicates; the extension is what makes the row interesting, since the borrowed syntax is being used to say something the source does not say. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold taken run by run.
9:14.text: He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.

provenance.route: Psalm 118:23, or Psalm 118:23 as quoted at Matthew 21:42 / Mark 12:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon; undecidable on this verse
provenance.mt: Psalm 118:23 — 'This is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.'
provenance.other: “marvellous in our eyes” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 118:23 and its two Synoptic quotations at Matthew 21:42 and Mark 12:11. The KJV renders the Greek of the Gospels with the identical English it gives the Hebrew of the Psalm, so tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence at any point Mormon 9:16 reproduces and reports that the verse cannot settle its own mediation. The 1830 spells 'marvellous' twice, with the King James's double l, where the modern edition prints 'marvelous' (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: What the Psalm calls marvellous in our eyes is a rejection reversed — the stone the builders refused becoming the head of the corner — and the Synoptics quote it at the end of the parable of the wicked husbandmen, addressed to authorities who are about to reject the son. Moroni asks 'are not the things that God hath wrought, marvellous in our eyes?' of people who have decided that God works nothing. Recover the context and the question sharpens: the one thing the Psalm identifies as marvellous is precisely a work of God that its own witnesses failed to recognise. That is the accusation of Mormon 9 in a phrase, and it comes with the Synoptic setting attached — the same pericope-neighbourhood the chapter has been in since 9:8 (Mark 12:24-26 stands fourteen verses after Mark 12:11).

9:16.note: 'Behold, are not the things that God hath wrought, marvellous in our eyes?' Four words verbatim from a phrase that occurs in exactly three KJV verses, one Psalm and its two quotations, and the borrowed clause is turned from a statement into a rhetorical question — which is the grammatical move the whole of 9:15-19 runs on. Mediation is `uncertain` and honestly so: the KJV's English is identical in all three, so nothing in the words can decide it. The context argument favours the Synoptics, because Mormon 9:8-11 has demonstrably been working in Mark 12, but a context argument is not a verbal one and the field is left open.
9:16.text: This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.

provenance.other: “by the hands of the apostles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:12, 'And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people'. Acts 2:43 has the same fact in different words ('many wonders and signs were done by the apostles') and Acts 19:11 the same construction for one man ('God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul'), so the six-word phrase with the plural is Acts 5:12's alone. Mormon 9:18 keeps the phrase, the adjective 'many' and the participle 'wrought'.
provenance.significance: The verse Moroni takes is the one that says apostolic miracles were public and continuous — 'among the people', in Solomon's porch, in the temple, where anyone could see them. That is exactly the property his opponents deny is available any longer. And the immediate context of Acts 5 is the sequel: the apostles are arrested for it, and Gamaliel tells the council that a work of God cannot be overthrown. Mormon 9:26, 'who can stand against the works of the Lord?', is Gamaliel's question.

9:18.note: 'And there was many mighty miracles wrought by the hands of the apostles.' A King James singleton kept whole, with 'many' and 'wrought' from the same clause and only Luke's 'signs and wonders' exchanged for the chapter's own keyword, 'miracles'. The exchange matters: Moroni is not narrating Acts but arguing from it, and the substitution converts an account of what happened into an instance of the category under dispute. The 1830's 'there was many' for the modern 'there were many' is a first-edition reading with no bearing on the source.
9:18.text: And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; (and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.

provenance.route: Matthew 13:58 (with Mark 6:5-6) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “many mighty works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:58, 'And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief'; “because of their unbelief” occurs in exactly two, that verse and Mark 6:6. Mormon 9:18 has 'many mighty miracles' two verses earlier and Mormon 9:20 has the unbelief, so Matthew's single sentence is distributed across Moroni's argument in Matthew's own terms.
provenance.significance: This is the pivot of the chapter's answer and it is built on the one Gospel verse that reports miracles NOT happening. Moroni's opponents infer from the absence of miracles that God has changed; Matthew 13:58 supplies the alternative inference, that the absence is caused at the other end. Mark 6:5 makes the concession sharper still — 'he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk, and healed them' — which is the very act Mormon 9:24 will quote from Mark 16:18, so the one thing unbelief could not stop in Nazareth is the sign Moroni promises will follow believers. And Mark 16:14, two verses before the commission Moroni reproduces at 9:22, has the risen Christ upbraiding the eleven 'with their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they believed not'. The stratum is consistent: everywhere Moroni touches the Gospels in this chapter, unbelief is the thing that stops the work.

9:20.note: 'And the reason why he ceaseth to do miracles among the children of men, is because that they dwindle in unbelief.' No clause is reproduced — 'dwindle in unbelief' is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, used from 1 Nephi onward — which is why this is filed as conceptual allusion rather than verbal. What earns the row is that the proposition is a King James singleton's proposition, that Moroni has supplied its other half two verses earlier in the singleton's own words ('many mighty' + 'wrought'), and that he is three verses away from quoting the chapter of Mark in which the same charge is laid against the apostles themselves.
9:20.text: And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

provenance.route: John 16:23, with Acts 10:20 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “shall ask the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both John 16:23; John 15:16's nearest rival reads 'ask OF the Father in my name'. Separately, “doubting nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 10:20, and its inversion “nothing doubting” occurs in exactly one, Acts 11:12 — the two halves of Peter's account of being sent to Cornelius. Mark 11:23's 'shall not doubt in his heart' and James 1:6's 'ask in faith, nothing wavering' are the doctrinally nearer verses and neither supplies the phrase.
provenance.significance: The two singletons come from opposite ends of the New Testament and the join is the argument. John 16:23 is a promise made to disciples in the upper room, on the night before the crucifixion, about what will be possible after the resurrection; Acts 10:20 is the moment the promise is extended past Israel, when the Spirit tells Peter to go with Cornelius's men 'doubting nothing'. Moroni's sentence closes 'and this promise is unto all, even unto the ends of the earth' — his own generalising clause, made out of the two verses that most exactly mark the promise and its extension. He repeats 'doubting nothing' four verses later at 9:25, where it governs the promise Christ makes to whoever believes in his name, which makes the phrase the hinge of the chapter's closing pair of promises.

9:21.note: 'Whatsoever he shall ask the Father in the name of Christ, it shall be granted them.' Five words verbatim from a King James singleton with the possessive changed from Christ's first person to Moroni's third, and 'doubting nothing' — a second singleton, from Acts — set in front of it. The 1830's 'it shall be granted THEM' after a singular subject was regularised to 'him' in 1920; the plural is the first edition's and it is the reading that matches the sentence's next clause, 'this promise is unto all'.
9:21.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

provenance.other: “go ye into all the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “and preach the gospel to every creature” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Mark 16:15. Matthew's Great Commission (28:19) shares not one of these words; Mark's longer ending is the only place in the English Bible where this sentence exists.
provenance.significance: Everything about this quotation is decided by which Mark is being quoted. Mark 16:9-20 — the 'longer ending' — is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the two oldest complete Greek witnesses to the Gospel, and is marked as doubtful or bracketed in essentially every critical edition since Tischendorf. A modern reader meets it in a footnote. The King James Bible prints it as scripture without qualification, and Mormon 9:22-24 reproduces roughly fifty consecutive words of it. Moroni introduces them with 'thus saith Jesus Christ, the Son of God, unto his disciples which should tarry' — an attribution to the risen Christ of words that the manuscript tradition does not place in his mouth. Whatever one concludes from that, it is the strongest single instance of `kjvSpecific: yes` in the book: not merely the KJV's English but the KJV's canon.

9:22.note: Thirteen words reproduced without a variant from a verse containing two King James singletons, introduced by an explicit speech formula naming the speaker and the audience. This is the first of three consecutive verses (9:22-24) that quote Mark 16:15-18 continuously; taken together they run to about fifty words and comfortably exceed Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though nothing here should be read as a claim about which passages are on his list, which this project does not hold (PLAN §4.1). Hardy's apparatus records the whole span with the note that the wording exactly matches Mark 16:15-18, keying it — as his convention is — at the last verse of the span, 9:25; the link is filed here, where the wording is, and the register at 9:25 sends a reader back.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
9:22.text: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.

provenance.other: “he that believeth and is baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “believeth not shall be damned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Mark 16:16. The verse is reproduced entire and unaltered: seventeen consecutive words, with only the KJV's semicolon becoming a comma.
provenance.significance: This is the longest unbroken verbatim run in Mormon 9 and, at seventeen words, it clears the sixteen-word bar by which Skousen defines a King James quotation — a fact worth recording precisely because this catalogue does not adopt that threshold (CONVENTIONS §2) and can therefore state without special pleading that here it is met. The doctrinal weight is heavy for a text arguing about signs: the verse makes baptism a condition of salvation, and Moroni will spend 9:29 on receiving baptism and the sacrament worthily. And it belongs, like its neighbours, to Mark's longer ending — so the Book of Mormon's clearest statement that the unbeliever is damned rests on a passage the Greek manuscript tradition does not carry.

9:23.note: A whole KJV verse, seventeen words, word for word. There is nothing to adjudicate about the source and everything to notice about the frame: Moroni is quoting the risen Christ to prove that the gifts have not ceased, and the sentence he chooses is the one that makes belief the hinge — which is the same claim he made in his own voice at 9:20, that miracles stop where unbelief begins. Cited by Hardy as part of the 9:22-25 span; see the note at 9:22 on his keying.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
9:23.text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.

provenance.other: “these signs shall follow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “signs shall follow”; “speak with new tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All three are Mark 16:17, and Mormon 9:24 reproduces the verse entire, twenty-two words, with the KJV's semicolon after 'believe' becoming a colon.
provenance.significance: The list Moroni quotes here is the answer to the list he put in his opponents' mouths at 9:7. There they deny 'gifts, nor healing, nor speaking with tongues, and the interpretation of tongues', which is Paul's inventory from 1 Corinthians 12:9-10; here he supplies Christ's own inventory from Mark 16:17-18, and the two overlap at tongues and at healing. That is the shape of the whole argument: a Pauline list is denied and a dominical list is produced against it, and the dominical one comes with a promise attached — 'these signs SHALL follow' — that the Pauline one, read through 1 Corinthians 13:10, was being used to cancel.

9:24.note: A whole KJV verse reproduced, containing three King James singletons. The 1830 capitalises 'Devils' where the King James does not, which is a compositor's habit rather than a reading. This verse and the next together carry the chapter's title claim — that the signs of Mark's longer ending are still on offer — and the run from 9:22 through the end of this verse is about fifty consecutive words of a passage that is absent from the oldest Greek witnesses to Mark. Part of the span Hardy cross-references at 9:25.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
9:24.text: And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues;

provenance.other: Four King James singletons in one verse. “take up serpents” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “deadly thing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “lay hands on the sick” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “and they shall recover” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All four are Mark 16:18. Mormon 9:24 reproduces the verse entire, twenty-eight words, unaltered.
provenance.significance: Mark 16:18 is the most textually disputed sentence in the Gospel's most textually disputed paragraph, and it is reproduced here without a word out of place. Two of its four signs — serpent-handling and the harmless poison — have no other warrant anywhere in scripture and no counterpart in the Book of Mormon's own narrative; nothing in Nephite history involves either. They are here because the verse is here. That is an argument about mechanism rather than about doctrine, and it is why this row and its three neighbours are the chapter's centre of gravity: the borrowing includes material the borrower has no independent use for.

9:24.note: Twenty-eight consecutive words, four King James singletons, not a variant between the two texts. Catalogued as a separate row from Mark 16:17 because each is a whole verse quoted whole, and a reader looking up either should find the full source text against it; together they are one continuous quotation occupying the whole of Mormon 9:24. Part of the span Hardy cross-references at 9:25 with the observation that the wording exactly matches; the keying convention is discussed at 9:22.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
9:24.text: They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.

provenance.route: Habakkuk 1:5 → the Septuagint → Acts 13:41 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Habakkuk 1:5 — 'Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvelously: for I will work a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you.'
provenance.lxx: Acts 13:41 quotes Habakkuk in its Greek form, which reads 'despisers' where the Hebrew has 'among the nations' (bogedim for baggoyim) and 'perish' (aphanisthete) where the Hebrew has 'wonder marvellously'. The KJV translates each from its own base, so the two English verses diverge exactly where the Greek and Hebrew do.
provenance.other: “wonder and perish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:41; the Old Testament's corresponding phrase, “wonder marvelously”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Habakkuk 1:5. “despisers” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 13:41 and 2 Timothy 3:3. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both for Acts: the Book of Mormon has Acts's 'despisers', not Habakkuk's 'among the heathen and regard', and Acts's 'and perish', not Habakkuk's 'marvelously'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's cleanest mediation finding and one of the cleanest in the book, because the two candidate verses differ at precisely the two points Mormon 9:26 reproduces, and the Book of Mormon has the Greek side of both. The route is therefore not merely 'via the New Testament' in a loose sense: it runs through a Septuagint reading that the Hebrew does not support, which reaches English only because Paul quoted it at Antioch and the KJV translated Paul's Greek. A text presenting itself as an independent Israelite record has here the Septuagint's misreading of Habakkuk, in Luke's framing of it, in the King James's English. And the setting is apt to the point of comment: Acts 13:41 is the last sentence of Paul's first recorded sermon, the closing warning of a synagogue address that immediately precedes the turn to the Gentiles — which is the position Mormon 9:26-27 occupies at the close of Moroni's own last address to unbelievers.

9:26.note: 'Behold, all ye that are despisers of the works of the Lord, for ye shall wonder and perish.' Not a long run, but every word of it is the New Testament's rather than the Old Testament's at the two places where the Testaments disagree, and the next verse continues the engagement in Moroni's own voice — 'O then despise not, and wonder not' — taking up both of the borrowed verbs and negating them. That continuation is what raises this above a chance echo: the source's two distinctive words are used twice, once as accusation and once as counsel. Filed as quotation on the completeness of the reproduced clause and high rather than certain because the run is short.
9:26.text: Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.

provenance.other: “work out your own salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 2:12; the trailing “with fear and trembling” occurs in exactly three, of which that is one, so the nine-word run as a whole is unique. The same verse's 'as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence' is the frame Moroni's own 9:30 will echo — 'I speak unto you as though I spake from the dead'.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about what a congregation must do when its apostle is not there. Moroni's whole colophon is written from precisely that position and pressed to its limit: not absent but dead, addressing readers separated from him by centuries rather than by miles, who cannot ask him anything. Recover Philippians 2:12 and the borrowing supplies the reason the exhortation takes this form — 'not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence' is the premise of Mormon 9:30-31, where Moroni asks not to be condemned for imperfections no one can now correct. The nine borrowed words carry an argument about absence that Moroni never states.

9:27.note: 'And work out your own salvation with fear and trembling before him.' Nine consecutive words from a King James singleton, with 'before him' added. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold but a complete reproduced predicate, which is what decides the category under CONVENTIONS §2. The verse also returns to John 16:23 — 'ask the Father in the name of Jesus for what things soever ye shall stand in need' — already catalogued at 9:21, and its opening 'O then despise not, and wonder not' continues the Acts 13:41 borrowing catalogued at 9:26.
9:27.text: Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.

provenance.other: “consume it upon your lusts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:3, and the shorter “may consume it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon reads 'consume it ON your lusts' for the KJV's 'upon', which is the only difference in six words.
provenance.significance: James 4:3 is the New Testament's one statement that a prayer can be answered with a refusal on grounds of motive — 'ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss'. Moroni has just issued, at 9:21, an unrestricted promise that whatever is asked of the Father in Christ's name will be granted, and at 9:27 has told his readers to ask for whatever they stand in need of. This verse is the qualification, and he takes it from the one verse in the Bible that qualifies exactly that promise. The pair is a small piece of pastoral engineering: the promise and its limit are both quoted, from John and from James, seven verses apart.

9:28.note: 'Ask not, that ye may consume it on your lusts, but ask with a firmness unshaken.' Six words from a King James singleton with one preposition changed, and the second half of the sentence answers James 1:6 ('let him ask in faith, nothing wavering') in Moroni's own vocabulary rather than the KJV's — 'a firmness unshaken' for 'nothing wavering', where the KJV's own figure is a wave driven by the wind. Filed as allusion rather than quotation because the borrowed words are a subordinate clause rather than a predicate.
9:28.text: Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.

provenance.other: “in no wise cast out” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:37, 'him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out'. The bare “in no wise” occurs in exactly eleven verses, so the phrase is identified by its verb. The 1830 prints 'in no wise' as two words where the modern edition has 'nowise', which preserves the King James spacing (CONVENTIONS §8). 'Endure to the end' is the Book of Mormon's standing form of Matthew 10:22's 'endureth to the end'; “endure unto the end” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, and “endure to the end” occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: John 6:37 is a promise about admission, made in the discourse on the bread of life — the chapter in which Jesus identifies himself as the bread and says that whoever eats it has eternal life. Moroni's sentence is about the sacrament: 'see that ye partake not of the sacrament of Christ unworthily … and if ye do this, and endure to the end, ye will in no wise be cast out.' So the promise is taken from the one chapter of the Gospels where eating and being received are the same subject, and it is turned into the reassurance that follows a warning about eating unworthily. The warning itself is Paul's (1 Corinthians 11:27-29) and the reassurance is John's; Moroni does not name either.

9:29.note: Five words from a King James singleton, made passive — Christ's 'I will in no wise cast out' becomes 'ye will in no wise be cast out', which removes the speaker and leaves the guarantee. The conditional attached to it, 'if ye do this, and endure to the end', is the Book of Mormon's regular adaptation of Matthew 10:22 and is not itself a KJV phrase in that form.
9:29.text: All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.

provenance.route: Ezekiel 33:6 → Acts 18:6 and Acts 20:26 → KJV → Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 2:2, Mosiah 2:28) → Mormon 9:35
provenance.other: “your blood be upon your own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6, where Paul shakes his raiment at the synagogue at Corinth and says 'I am clean'; “pure from the blood” and “blood of all men” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:26, the farewell at Miletus. Neither KJV verse contains the Book of Mormon's actual phrase, which is 'rid our garments of the blood'; that formula is the Book of Mormon's own, and it occurs at 2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 2:2, Mosiah 2:28 and here.
provenance.significance: This is the fifth and last link in a chain the catalogue has been following since 2 Nephi, and it is the one that closes the book. Jacob takes off his garments and shakes them (2 Nephi 9:44); Jacob comes to the temple to rid his garments of the people's sins (Jacob 2:2); Benjamin gathers his people to rid his garments of their blood before going down to his grave (Mosiah 2:28); Moroni writes to rid the garments of the record's authors — 'we', plural, his father and himself and those before them — of the blood of a people already destroyed. The proximate model is not the King James but Mosiah 2:28, a page Mormon himself abridged, and the difference in each recasting is what the gesture is performed against: Benjamin has an audience in front of him, Moroni has only a book. `mediation` is recorded as `direct-NT` because the enum has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; the route field carries what the enum cannot, and this is flagged for the conventions rather than solved here (CONVENTIONS §7 provides OT-via-earlier-BoM only).

9:35.note: 'And these things are written, that we may rid our garments of the blood of our brethren which have dwindled in unbelief.' No King James words survive, which is why the type is conceptual: what survives is a gesture that the KJV performs once, at Acts 18:6, and a liability that it states once, at Acts 20:26, and behind both the watchman of Ezekiel 33:6 whose hand the blood is required at. The catalogue has filed Acts 18:6 at 2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 2:2 and Mosiah 2:28 already; this row records the last occurrence and the fact that its immediate model is Nephite rather than biblical. The object of the gesture has changed one last time — Benjamin rids his garments of the blood of the living, Moroni of the blood of the dead.
9:35.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “prayers of all saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 8:3, where an angel offers incense with them at the golden altar; the variant “prayers of the saints” occurs in exactly one, the following verse, and Revelation 5:8 has 'the prayers of saints' in the vials of the elders. Mormon 9:36 reads 'the prayers of all the saints which have dwelt in the land', which is Revelation 8:3's phrase with the article added.
provenance.significance: Revelation 8:3-4 is the moment the accumulated prayers of the whole church go up together and the seventh seal's silence ends; what follows immediately is fire cast on the earth. Moroni's last request before the book's closing benediction is that the restoration of his brethren should happen 'according to the prayers of all the saints which have dwelt in the land' — the prayers of the dead of a destroyed civilisation, gathered and still pending. Recover the context and the sentence acquires a mechanism: the prayers are not lost with the people who prayed them, because in the source they are held at an altar until they are offered. The chapter has already taken Revelation 22:11 at 9:14 and stands before John's throne at 9:2; this is consistent with the book's closing pages being written with the Apocalypse open.

9:36.note: Five words from a King James singleton, and no other contact with Revelation 8. Filed as an echo at moderate confidence because 'the prayers of the saints' is a phrase a devout writer might produce unprompted, and because the row rests entirely on rarity plus the Revelation stratum elsewhere in the chapter. It goes in under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth putting on the table: the significance, if the link holds, is that Moroni's last petition is made on the assumption that the prayers of his exterminated people are still in hand.
9:36.whyNot: Five words with no syntactic or contextual reproduction. The saints in Revelation 8 are the whole church at the end of history; Moroni's are the inhabitants of one land, and the KJV phrase without 'the' is close enough to ordinary devotional English that a writer could reach it by no route at all.
9:36.text: And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne.

provenance.other: “remember the covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 26:45; Leviticus 26:42 has 'remember my covenant' three times over and 'I will remember the land'. Luke 1:72's “his holy covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is the New Testament's nearest form. Mormon 9:37's actual wording — 'remember the covenant which he hath made with the house of Israel' — is not any of these; it is Mormon 5:20's wording, 'then will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham, and unto all the house of Israel', with Abraham dropped.
provenance.significance: The catalogue filed Leviticus 26:42 at Mormon 5:20, where Mormon states the promise after the scattering and before the restoration, exactly where Leviticus 26 places it. Mormon 9:37 is Moroni, finishing his father's book, closing it with his father's sentence in his father's order and one clause shorter. That is the small finding here and it is worth a row: the last verse of the book of Mormon is a benediction built out of the abridger's own formula, not out of the Bible directly, and `mediation` is `OT-via-earlier-BoM` on that account — the proximate model is a Book of Mormon page, and it happens to be a page by the man Moroni is burying.

9:37.note: 'And may God the Father remember the covenant which he hath made with the house of Israel.' No King James phrase survives intact — the covenant-remembering formula of Leviticus 26 is diffuse and the wording is Mormon 5:20's — so the row is filed as a conceptual echo and `kjvSpecific` as uncertain. It earns its place by the recurrence rather than by the vocabulary: the same clause, minus one member, from the same book, in the mouth of the son rather than the father, as the last petition of the last verse.
9:37.whyNot: Covenant-remembering language is spread across Leviticus, Psalms, Ezekiel and Luke, and a writer closing a book about Israel's restoration will reach for it without a source. The link to Mormon 5:20 is stronger than the link to Leviticus, and a reader who declines the Leviticus end of the chain will still have the internal repetition, which is the part that is actually demonstrable.
9:37.text: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land.
